resources.string: Spektrafilm renders your photos through a physically-modelled film stock and darkroom print — spectrum-accurate, not a preset filter.
Pick a photo or RAW/DNG → choose a film stock and a print paper → tune the look (grain, halation, couplers, glare) → export at full resolution.
A bit-exact port of the spektrafilm spectral pipeline, RAW decoding via LibRaw, and an Image-Toolbox-inspired Compose UI. Previews are downscaled for speed; exports render at full resolution.

Spektrafilm is a physically-based spectral film simulator. Unlike a simple filter or a look-up table, it models the real analog pipeline: a virtual negative is exposed to your photo\'s light, developed in a chemical bath, optionally enlarged onto print paper in a darkroom, and scanned back to a digital file — all driven by measured spectral data from real film stocks.
The result is a faithful reproduction of color, grain, halation, and dye chemistry that matches what you would get in a real darkroom — not an approximation.
Film modeling powered by spektrafilm (Andrea Volpato).
Tap the open button (top-left of the editor) to pick an image.
Choose a JPEG or HEIC from your gallery for quick results.
For the truest film rendering, open a RAW or DNG file. The app decodes RAW files through LibRaw to a linear, scene-referred image — the same starting point real film would have.
If you don\'t have a photo handy, tap \"Demo image\" to load the built-in test image.
EXIF orientation is read automatically: portrait shots and rotated RAW files will appear upright in the preview without you doing anything.
The editor is designed like a professional photo editing app. From top to bottom:

Pinned preview — your photo, rendered live with the current settings, fills the top portion of the screen. A status pill in the corner shows when a render is in progress and how long the last render took.
Histogram — displayed over the preview so you can judge exposure and clipping.
Scrollable category bar — a row of icons at the bottom. Swipe left/right to reach all 13 categories. Tap any icon to open that category\'s adjustment panel.
Tap a category icon to open its panel below the preview. Swipe the panel downward to dismiss it and return to the full preview.
open / close a photo, demo image, before/after compare
load a built-in or saved parameter set
film stock, print paper, exposure, Auto-exposure
grain amount, scale, sublayer mixing, 100% magnifier
lens flare / glare (print path, off by default)
developer options and advanced engine flags
output color space (sRGB, Adobe RGB, ProPhoto, Rec.2020, etc.)
Start here to find the right film character for your photo:

Open the Simulation category. Choose a film stock from the Film picker — 28 profiles are available, grouped as color negative, slide, motion-picture, and print film. Each profile shows the film\'s ISO, color balance, and era.
If you want a printed look (negative→enlarger→paper), also select a print paper in the Print picker within Simulation. Leave it at its default for a direct scan-of-the-negative result.

Adjust the exposure slider to brighten or darken the simulated exposure. Alternatively, tap Auto to let the app meter the scene for you. Auto-exposure meters to a mid-grey target and offers 7 metering patterns (center-weighted, matrix, spot, and more) in a pop-up list.
For a fast starting point, open the Presets category. 20 built-in, researched film-to-print looks are available. Tap a preset to load its full parameter set, then fine-tune from there.
Several tools are available directly in the editor:
90° rotate — the rotate button (top bar) rotates your photo 90° clockwise. The rotation applies to the preview, the export, and the grain magnifier.
Crop — the Input category contains an interactive crop overlay. Drag the corner and edge handles to crop freely, or tap one of the aspect ratio presets (1:1, 4:3, 3:2, 16:9, etc.) to lock the ratio.
Before / after compare — available in the Source category. Lets you flick between the original and the simulated result to judge the effect.
100% grain magnifier — accessible from the Grain category. Shows a 1:1 crop of the grain texture so you can check the grain scale and character before exporting at full resolution.

Profile curve browser — in the Simulation category, tap the film or paper name to open the curve browser. It shows that stock\'s spectral sensitivity, characteristic (H-D) density curves, and dye density spectra.
When a RAW or DNG file is loaded, the RAW WB category becomes active. It gives you control over how LibRaw interprets the raw sensor data:
Mode — choose As-shot (uses the camera\'s recorded white balance), Daylight, or Tungsten for a preset. Select Custom to enter your own values.
Temperature and Tint sliders — available in Custom mode to dial in a precise white balance. Changing either slider re-decodes the RAW preview automatically.
Reset — returns the white balance to the camera\'s as-shot setting.
For JPEG or HEIC sources the RAW WB category is hidden, since the white balance is already baked into those files.
All edits are non-destructive. Here is what that means in practice:
Your original file is never changed. The app only reads it.
Every adjustment is stored as a recipe (a small JSON sidecar) keyed to that specific source image.
When you reopen the same image later, the recipe is loaded automatically and the simulation re-renders exactly where you left off.
The recipe is re-applied at full resolution when you export, so your preview at a smaller size and the exported file at full resolution are the same look.
When you are happy with the look, tap the export button (top bar) to save the result.

Format — choose from 8-bit JPEG, 8-bit PNG, 16-bit TIFF, 16-bit PNG, or Google Ultra HDR (gain-map JPEG, on supported devices). 16-bit TIFF and 16-bit PNG preserve the full dynamic range of the simulation.
JPEG quality — a 0–100 slider for JPEG exports.
Keep GPS / location — OFF by default for privacy. Turn it on if you want GPS coordinates copied from the source EXIF into the exported file.
The exported file is saved to Pictures/Spektrafilm on your device. Camera metadata (make, model, lens, exposure settings) from the source image is copied into the exported file\'s EXIF automatically.
Judge film looks in a darkened room. Film character is subtle and ambient light on the screen will flatten your perception of it.
Use RAW input for the most accurate result. JPEG files have already been processed by the camera\'s tone curve, white balance, and sharpening, which changes how the simulation perceives the scene.
Export to 16-bit TIFF or 16-bit PNG when you plan to do further editing. This keeps the full precision of the simulation for later adjustments.
Auto-exposure meters to mid-grey. If your subject is lighter or darker than mid-grey you may want to nudge the exposure slider manually afterward.
Grain is stochastic (random). The preview may look slightly different each time you render; the export is always the definitive full-resolution version.

Film modeling powered by spektrafilm (Andrea Volpato). The science, the film-stock profiles, and the spectral LUTs are Andrea\'s work — Spektrafilm is a native Android port of that engine, verified bit-exact against the original.
UI inspired by Image Toolbox (T8RIN). Colour math from colour-science. RAW decoding via LibRaw. Free software under the GPLv3.
Applied when the app starts. Per-image edits and presets still override these.
Long edge of the interactive preview, in pixels.
Long edge of the fast frame drawn while a slider is being dragged, before the crisp render lands. Lower tracks your finger more closely; higher previews the final result more faithfully.
Off: strip GPS from exports (recommended). Other EXIF (camera, exposure, date) is always kept.

Render the fit preview instantly on the GPU (a 3D LUT of the current look) instead of a ~1s CPU render per edit. Export is always the exact CPU engine. Off by default: the current surface can stutter or overlap the controls while panels animate — being reworked.

Run the film simulation\'s scan stage on the GPU for interactive previews — more accurate than the preview LUT and verified against the CPU engine on this device at first use, with automatic CPU fallback. Export always uses the exact CPU engine. Applies on the next return to the editor.

Also run the scan stage on the GPU for full-resolution exports — \"oracle-verified on your device\": the result is checked against the CPU engine on this device and falls back to CPU automatically if it ever drifts. Off by default. Independent of the preview toggle.

Nothing is uploaded automatically. Reports include app/device version, redact paths, URIs and image metadata, and keep the last crash for at most 7 days. Copy or Share is always an explicit action.
